extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and critical thinkers evaluating arguments
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, classify, and diagnose errors in reasoning (inductive and deductive), focusing on five major classes of fallacy and many common a priori mistakes; supply suppressed premises and judge whether evidence supports conclusions. Useful for critiquing arguments in philosophy, science, and everyday discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation (Fallacies of Induction founded on erroneous facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive errors that arise when the facts on which the induction proceeds are erroneous — due to malobservation, simple non-observation, or inference from intermediate marks that do not prove what they are supposed to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as failures to ascertain the facts adequately. Includes direct bad observation and errors from inferring facts incorrectly. Detect by checking the empirical basis: were the observed instances accurate, sufficient, and properly interpreted? Examples: misreading signs, mistaking uncertain marks for certain evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization (correct facts but unwarranted conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where the facts themselves are correct but the generalization drawn from them is not warranted by that evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for overgeneralizing from limited or non-representative instances, concluding a single cause from an observed effect when multiple causes are possible, or drawing broad laws from inadequate samples. Example: concluding a government is tyrannical from general distress without adequate middle term distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination (deductive errors where premises don't support conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of incorrect deduction in which the premises (though perhaps true) do not bear out the conclusion; the various cases of vicious syllogistic argumentation contrary to rules of the syllogism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check syllogistic form and distribution of terms. Test whether the asserted middle term actually connects premises to conclusion. Supply omitted steps to see whether the chain of inference is valid. Distinguish from mere false premises (which may instead be inductive fallacies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors due to failure to state the question properly, inability to apprehend evidence with definiteness and precision, or other forms of conceptual confusion (including circular reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify as Confusion when neglect or inability to define terms and premises is the main cause. Detect by making implicit assumptions explicit; identify muddled or ambiguous concepts. Includes reasoning in a circle and cases where premises were never distinctly conceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (A priori fallacies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions embraced as self-evident or requiring no proof (assumed a priori) and accepted without adequate empirical support; mistakes arising from treating mental intuitions or subjective convictions as objective truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims taken as 'self-evident'. Ask what evidence would justify them and whether the assertion is actually an intuitively-held idea misapplied to external reality. The topic spans many subtypes (see below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking subjective ideas for objective properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that properties of our ideas (how we conceive things) are properties of the things themselves — e.g., treating laws of thought as laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between features of mental representation and features of external objects. Beware inferring ontological claims from introspective content. Example: assuming because we always think two things together they must co-exist in the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming conceivability implies possibility or truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that what can be very clearly and distinctly conceived must be true, or conversely that what is inconceivable must be impossible or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject using conceivability as a proof of actuality. Historical counterexamples (antipodes, Copernican system, gravitation acting at a distance) show that limits of imagination do not entail limits of reality. Consider whether apparent inconceivability is merely a limitation of current experience or imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming things thought together must co-exist (confusing association in thought with causal/coexistential relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of inferring that because two items are habitually thought of together, they must be concomitant in reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require empirical verification of supposed concomitance. Examples: omens and superstitions where ideas associated in the mind are taken as prognostics or causes; e.g., talking of the devil allegedly causing appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification or reification of abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating names or abstract general terms (Chance, Nature, Time, Fate, 'man in general') as if they denote distinct, separable entities (universals considered as substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that a linguistic or conceptual generality corresponds to a distinct object. Analyze whether the term denotes a class of phenomena or an independent entity. Recognize this tendency under 'mysticism' in metaphysical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of the Principle of Sufficient Reason (assuming absence of a reason implies impossibility of variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing that if there is no reason why a phenomenon should vary in one way rather than another, then it will not vary (used to infer e.g., inertia from lack of apparent reason to move in a particular direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question the hidden premise that external reason is the only possible cause; treat such arguments as petitio principii unless supported by empirical evidence. Example: early arguments for a body's remaining at rest because no reason exists to move it in any particular direction are fallacious without independent justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to simplicity as proof ('nature acts by the simplest means')
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the hypothesis easiest to conceive or most simple must be the truest account of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity is heuristic but not conclusive. Historical mistakes (epicycles, circles for celestial motion) show that apparent simplicity can mask complexity; require empirical confirmation rather than privileging conceivability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressed or tacit premises and the method of detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Many erroneous arguments have suppressed links or premises; to detect the fallacy one must supply the tacit premise and test it (it will be either untrue or fail to prove the conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection technique: make implicit premises explicit (Socratic interrogation), then evaluate whether the supplied premise is true or whether it merely yields an unsound syllogism. Whately's example: assess whether the speaker intends a false premise or an unsound syllogism, and note that hearers may supply different premises leading to different classifications of the fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies cluster and classification can be ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual erroneous arguments often embody multiple fallacies or can be assigned to different classes depending on how suppressed premises are filled; one fallacy may pave the way for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying, choose the seat of the fallacy most probable given the nature of the evidence and tendencies of the mind in the situation; acknowledge that strict, mutually-exclusive classification is often impossible and that practical utility of distinctions is the goal.
